title: U.N. Halts Strait of Hormuz Evacuation After Cargo Ship Is Attacked, Stranding Thousands of Sailors Again
excerpt: A drone strike on a tanker off Oman forces the IMO to suspend a rescue that had just freed 1,100 seafarers, reviving fears for the fragile U.S.-Iran deal and the Indians who crew the world's ships.
body:
The rescue lasted barely two days. On Thursday the United Nations' shipping agency abruptly **paused the evacuation of more than 11,000 seafarers stranded in the Strait of Hormuz** after a cargo ship was attacked in the Gulf of Oman, plunging one of the world's busiest energy corridors back into the uncertainty it had only just begun to escape.

The vessel, identified by four sources as the Singapore-flagged *Ever Lovely*, reported being struck by a projectile close to the coast of Oman, Britain's UKMTO naval agency said. A maritime security source said it was likely hit by a drone. The strike damaged the ship's bridge but caused no casualties. It came only hours after Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned vessels not to use routes through the waterway that Tehran had not sanctioned — and two senior U.S. officials told the *Wall Street Journal* the IRGC itself was responsible.

**An operation undone within hours**

The evacuation had been launched only on Tuesday, the product of months of painstaking diplomacy. It offered ships a voluntary, escorted way out of the Gulf along two tracks: a northern route through Iranian waters and a southern route through Omani waters under U.S. oversight. By Thursday morning, initial IMO data showed **57 ships carrying an estimated 1,100 seafarers had already transited safely** between June 23 and June 25 — the first real movement since the strait effectively closed when war erupted in late February.

Then came the attack, and with it the reversal.

[X_EMBED:2070211803146055970]

"I have been informed of an attack today in the Gulf of Oman on a vessel which passed through the Strait of Hormuz. This vessel did not transit under IMO's evacuation framework," Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez said in a statement, stressing that the targeted ship was not part of the rescue. "I have decided to temporarily pause its implementation in order to reconfirm that the necessary safety guarantees continue to be in place for the ships on our evacuation list and all those in the region."

The pause is a heavy blow. Before the conflict, the Strait of Hormuz carried roughly a fifth of the world's daily oil and liquefied natural gas. Traffic had been recovering fast — ship trackers counted 70 to 80 vessels passing the chokepoint on Wednesday, the highest level since the war began. The incident off Oman threatens to freeze that recovery in place.

**Markets flinch, and a fragile deal wobbles**

Benchmark oil prices rose 1.9% after the reported attack, with analysts warning it rekindled doubts about how long it could take for Gulf flows to return to normal. The deeper worry is political. The 60-day agreement signed last week between Washington and Tehran requires Iran to make its "best efforts" to ensure safe passage for commercial vessels in return for the lifting of the U.S. blockade of its ports; as part of the pact, the United States waived sanctions on Iranian oil sales and allowed Tehran to sell crude in dollars for the first time in decades. An attack attributed to the IRGC — days into that bargain — tests whether the deal can hold at all. The White House did not immediately comment.

The episode also sharpens a question that has hung over the strait for months: how much control Iran intends to exert over who passes and on what terms. Tehran recently stood up a new Persian Gulf Strait Authority, since sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury, that Washington accuses of extorting tolls from commercial shipping. Thursday's warning against "unapproved" routes, followed by a strike, reads to many shipowners as an answer.

**Why this lands hard on Indian families**

For India, this is not an abstract freight story. India is the world's single largest supplier of merchant seafarers, and earlier reporting put the number of Indians caught on ships in the Gulf at roughly 18,000. The human cost is already real: **three Indian sailors were killed** when a commercial vessel was caught in an attack near the strait earlier this month, among at least 14 seafarers who have died since the crisis began. Every paused transit means another stretch of waiting for crews who have now spent four months at anchor — and another stretch of anxiety for the remittance-dependent households back home in Kerala, Goa, Andhra Pradesh and Maharashtra that depend on their wages.

There is also the pump-price dimension that touches every diaspora family with ties to India. The country imports more than 85% of its crude, and a sustained spike in Hormuz risk premiums feeds directly into India's import bill, the rupee and domestic fuel costs.

**What happens next**

The IMO has framed the suspension as temporary — a pause to "reconfirm" safety guarantees rather than an abandonment. Dominguez has long insisted the evacuation can only proceed when all parties provide credible assurances against attacks and when hazards, including suspected mines in the traffic separation scheme, are cleared. Whether those guarantees can survive a strike attributed to Iran's own forces is now the central test, both of the rescue and of the wider peace it was meant to symbolize. For the seafarers still riding at anchor in the Gulf tonight, the way home has narrowed once more.
image_caption: A tanker lies at anchor waiting to enter port. Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz had begun to recover before Thursday's attack forced the U.N. to pause its evacuation.
